title: Tofu Pad Thai
changes_from_base: Prawns and fish sauce left out; 400 g pressed tofu, fried until crisp, and soy sauce in the tamarind sauce.
summary: This vegetarian pad thai follows the classic prawn and tofu method, but leaves out the prawns and fish sauce, uses soy sauce in the tamarind sauce, and fries a larger batch of pressed tofu until crisp.
equipment: wok (35 cm) or large non-stick frying pan (30 cm)
small bowls for the prepared ingredients

ingredients.item: dried flat rice noodles (3-5 mm wide)
palm sugar, chopped, or light brown sugar
extra-firm tofu, patted dry, in 1.5 cm cubes
garlic chives or spring onion greens, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.title: Press the tofu
steps.text: This vegetarian version follows the same soak, sauce and stir-fry method as the classic prawn and tofu pad thai, swapping soy sauce for fish sauce and using a bigger batch of tofu in place of prawns. Wrap the tofu in a folded tea towel, set a weight on top and leave it for 15 minutes before cooking. Pressing out the moisture means the tofu browns properly and holds its shape in the wok rather than steaming and falling apart.

steps.title: Soak the noodles
steps.text: Cover the rice noodles with hot tap water and leave to soak for 20-30 minutes, separating the strands with your fingers now and then. They're ready once they're white and bendy but still firm at the centre, since they finish cooking later in the sauce. Soaking rather than boiling keeps them from turning mushy once they hit the hot wok.

steps.title: Make the tamarind sauce
steps.text: Soak the tamarind pulp in the boiling water for 10 minutes, then mash it and push it through a sieve, scraping the underside to catch all the pulp, and discard the seeds and fibres. Stir in the palm sugar and soy sauce and warm for 1-2 minutes until the sugar has fully dissolved. Taste for the sour-salty-sweet balance that makes the sauce work.

steps.title: Line everything up
steps.text: Set the pressed tofu, garlic, shallot, egg, noodles and sauce out in the order you'll need them, with a mug of hot water nearby. The cooking itself moves quickly, so there's no time to start chopping once the wok is hot. Use two batches if your pan is smaller than 35cm, since overcrowding steams the noodles instead of frying them.

steps.title: Fry the tofu
steps.text: Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the wok over high and fry the tofu in two batches for 4-5 minutes each, until golden and crisp at the edges. Lift each batch out once it's coloured and firm. Frying in batches rather than all at once stops the tofu steaming in its own moisture and keeps the crisp edges you just built.

steps.title: Toss noodles in sauce
steps.text: Add 1 tablespoon of oil to the wok with the garlic and shallot and stir for 20-30 seconds until fragrant. Tip in the noodles and sauce and toss for 2-3 minutes, adding hot water a tablespoon at a time if things look dry, until the noodles are tender and have taken on an even golden colour from the soy sauce, the sign that they've absorbed the sauce rather than sitting in a pool of it.

steps.title: Scramble in the egg
steps.text: Push the noodles to one side, pour in the last of the oil and add the eggs. Leave them for about 20 seconds to set at the base, then scramble and fold through the noodles. Letting the egg firm up slightly before mixing keeps it in soft curds rather than vanishing into wet strands.

steps.title: Return tofu and sprouts
steps.text: Return the crisp tofu to the wok with the bean sprouts and garlic chives, and toss for about 30 seconds. The sprouts should still have some crunch left when it's time to serve.

steps.title: Serve with peanuts and lime
steps.text: Divide between plates and finish with the chopped peanuts, lime wedges and chilli flakes alongside. The lime's sharpness cuts through the rich tofu and sauce, and the peanuts add crunch to every mouthful. Serve straight away before the noodles start to firm up.

tips: Don't skip pressing the tofu — tofu straight from the packet holds too much water and won't brown, it'll just steam in the pan.
Fry the tofu in two batches rather than crowding the wok, or it will sweat rather than crisp.
Scrape the underside of the sieve when straining the tamarind, as a lot of the pulp clings there and gets left behind otherwise.
Keep all your ingredients measured out before you start, since the stir-fry stage moves too fast to pause and prep.
storage: Store in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat in a hot wok or microwave until piping hot throughout, loosening with a splash of water if needed. Freezing isn't recommended, as the noodles and bean sprouts lose their texture once thawed. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
